response: Code-switching, the use of more than one language within a single utterance, is a ubiquitous phenomenon in much of the world, particularly in multilingual communities. Code-switching can take many forms, including intersentential switching, where a speaker switches languages between sentences, and intrasentential switching, where a speaker switches languages within a sentence (Poplack, 1980). While code-switching has been well-documented in linguistics and sociolinguistics, it has proven to be a significant challenge for Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems. One major reason for this difficulty is the lack of representative and annotated data for training NLP models (Qian et al., 1999). In particular, there is a paucity of publicly available labeled data for code-switched text, which hinders the development of effective machine learning models for code-switched text processing tasks. In this paper, we present a novel model architecture for part-of-speech (POS) tagging that can be applied to code-switched text without explicit language identification (i.e., without knowing the language of each word or sentence in advance). Inspired by recent advances in multilingual embedding models (e.g., Conneau et al., 2020), our approach jointly represents words from different languages (or scripts) in a shared space, allowing our model to predict POS tags without forcing it to commit to a particular language. In this way, our model can leverage monolingual resources for training, while still being capable of handling unseen code-switched text at inference time. We call our model the "Multi-Language POS Tagger" (MLPST), and outline its architecture in Fig. 1. At a high level, our model consists of a word representation module, a language representation module, and a POS tagging module. We first describe our word representation module (Section 2), which processes individual words from various languages (or scripts) in parallel and produces a shared embedding space. We then describe our language representation module (Section 3), which learns to predict the "language" of each word from its surrounding context. Finally, we describe our POS tagging module (Section 4), which utilizes the word representations and language probabilities produced by the previous modules to predict the POS of each word. We evaluate the MLPST on the task of POS tagging for code-switched Hindi-English text, which is one of the most commonly used language pairs in code-switching research (Kamunikaki et al., 2015). We draw upon a recently created annotated dataset, which includes balanced training and test sets of both monolingual Hindi and English text (Muhammad et al., 2017). Our experiments demonstrate that the MLPST significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines when trained on monolingual text without transliteration and tested on code-switched text with alternate scripts (Devanagari and Roman) (Section 5). response: Discourse parsing is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), which aims to identify the relationships between sentences or spans in a text document. Recent advances in deep learning have led to significant improvements in various NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis, question answering, and machine translation. However, discourse parsing remains a challenging task due to its complexity and variability in human communication. Specifically, discourse parsing involves identifying the hierarchical structure of a text document, including the relationships between discourse units (DU), such as sentences, paragraphs, and sections. Traditional approaches to discourse parsing have relied heavily on hand-engineered features and machine learning algorithms, which are often computationally expensive and require significant manual effort to construct. In recent years, deep learning-based approaches have gained popularity in the NLP community, including language modeling (LM), machine translation, and text classification. However, applying deep learning to discourse parsing has been less explored, primarily due to the complexity of the task and the availability of suitable datasets. In this paper, we propose an attention-based hierarchical neural network model for discourse parsing, which incorporates a tensor-based transformation function to capture complicated feature interactions. Central to our approach is the use of attention mechanisms, which have been successfully applied to various NLP tasks, including machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2014), text classification (Yin et al., 2016), and question answering (Seo et al., 2016). Attention mechanisms allow the model to focus on specific parts of the input sequence, which is particularly useful in discourse parsing, where the relationships between discourse units can be complex and nuanced. Our proposed model consists of two main components: a hierarchical neural network and a tensor-based transformation function. The hierarchical neural network takes as input the tokenized representation of the input text and outputs a representation of the discourse structure, including the relationships between discourse units. The tensor-based transformation function captures the complicated feature interactions between the input text and the discourse structure, which is essential for capturing the nuanced relationships between discourse units. We evaluate our approach on the Discourse Parsing (DST) dataset, which is a benchmark dataset for discourse parsing. Our experimental results show that our approach obtains comparable performance to the contemporary state-of-the-art systems with little manual feature engineering. Specifically, we achieve a competitiveness of 89.2% F1-score on the DST dataset, which is comparable to the state-of-the-art performance of 90.1% achieved by the first-place winning system in the CoNLL 2011 Shared Task. The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews the related work in discourse parsing and attention-based models. Section 3 presents our proposed approach, including the hierarchical neural network and the tensor-based transformation function. Section 4 discusses the experimental results, including the evaluation metrics and the comparison with related work. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and discusses the future work. response: Digital personal assistants, such as Siri, Alexa, and Google Assistant, have become an essential part of our daily lives. They have the ability to comprehend and execute various tasks based on user commands. However, the major challenge in developing such personal assistants is machine understanding, which involves translating natural language user commands into an executable representation that a computer can execute. This challenge is known as the semantic parsing task. In this paper, we focus on one of the most common natural language command formats used in this context - If-Then rules. If-Then rules are conditional statements that consist of an "if" condition and a corresponding "then" outcome. The "if" part is often a boolean expression, involving comparison of one or more entities. The "then" part, on the other hand, can involve various actions, such as changing a setting, sending a notification, or playing a piece of information. Semantic parsing, the task of transforming natural language into a machine-understandable representation, has been extensively studied in the community of natural language processing (NLP). In recent years, the focus has shifted from rule-based approaches, to more data-driven approaches, such as neural network models. Neural network models, often, generalize better to various tasks and data distributions than traditional rule-based models. These models are capable of learning complex representations of language, from sentences to predicates, and mapping these representations to executable representations. Structure prediction is a critical challenge in understanding If-Then rules, as the structure of the rule is what determines the meaning of the sentence. This means that the parser must correctly identify the entities involved in the "if" and "then" parts of the rule. Given the complexity of natural language, it is often unrealistic to expect that a single grammar can fully capture the range of possible structures. Rather, one typically uses a probability distribution over a set of grammars, reflecting our uncertainty in the true underlying grammar. In this problem, the goal is to induce a probabilistic grammar that can predict the meaning of any given sentence, thereby overcoming the limitations of manually constructed grammars and generalizing to novel domains. Some existing approaches have made significant progress in this area, although they are often tailored to specific natural languages or meaning representations (Zettlemoyer and Collins 2005;Hockenmaier and Steedman 2007;Artzi et al. 2012). However, these methods are typically designed to be language-dependent and data-specific, thereby limiting their applicability. Consequently, there is a pressing need for a more general and effective approach to inducing probabilistic CCG grammars from logical forms. One of the key requirements for addressing this problem is the ability to search a hypothesis space containing all grammars that are consistent with the training data. This space should be sufficiently large to ensure that it includes the "optimal" grammar, yet small enough to make the search computationally tractable. Our approach uses higher-order unification to achieve this goal. In particular, we generalize the notion of unification to higher-order logic, allowing us to characterize the hypothesis space using a combinatorial grammar formalism. A key challenge in maintaining and populating these KBs is the difficulty in incorporating new entities and updating existing information, a problem referred to as Knowledge Base Population (KBP). KBP involves several subtasks, including Cold Start Slot Filling (CSSF), where the goal is to extract a predefined set of attributes from text, and Tri-lingual Entity Discovery and Linking (TEDL), which involves identifying and linking entities across different languages. Supervised learning has been commonly used in KBP, relying heavily on manually annotated training data, which can be expensive and time-consuming to obtain. As an alternative, unsupervised methods, which can operate without labeled data, have recently gained popularity. However, an important limitation of these unsupervised methods is that their performance can be erratic and uncertain. Conversely, supervised methods can often provide reliable results but require extensive annotated data, limiting their applicability. Recent approaches have aimed to combine strengths from supervised and unsupervised methods through various ensemble techniques. Ensemble methods, such as stacking (Wolpert, 1992), have achieved impressive results in several NLP tasks, including KBP. By learning multiple models individually and combining their predictions, ensemble methods can leverage diverse strengths and compensate for individual weaknesses. We build upon these approaches, combining supervised and unsupervised ensembling for two prominent KBP tasks: CSSF and TEDL. Specifically, we enhance ensemble performance through these extensions: 1) Combination models based on neural networks; 2) Integration of multiple unsupervised algorithms with unified weighting; 3) Effective supervised ensemble weighted combinations. response: Error correction is a challenging task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), with a wide range of applications in education, human-computer interaction, and machine translation. There are numerous studies that have demonstrated the effectiveness of various machine learning algorithms for correcting errors in learners' writing, including language models (LM) (Kroehn et al., 2002), errorspecific classifiers (Bai and Carpuat, 2015), and hybrid approaches (Liu et al., 2014). However, the design of effective correction systems is often constrained by the availability of annotated data, which is typically either expensive to produce or difficult to obtain in sufficient quantities. Most state-of-the-art error correction systems rely heavily on large, pre-existing corpora of native English texts, often annotated with error information (G jets, 2003). The standard approach is to train a language model on this native corpus, using it to capture the statistical patterns of native English language use (Bai and Carpuat, 2015). However, this approach has several limitations. Firstly, it does not account for any errors that learners may make, which is the primary purpose of an error correction system. Secondly, it often relies on heavy feature engineering, requiring significant amounts of domain-specific knowledge. Furthermore, relying solely on large corpora of native English texts can result in inadequate error correction performance, particularly for errors that are common among non-native speakers. For instance, article and preposition errors, such as the use of "a" instead of "an" or the incorrect use of prepositions in phrases like "in the morning," are notoriously difficult to correct using language models alone (Kroehn et al., 2002). In this study, we explore a different approach to error correction, one that leverages the strengths of language models and errorspecific classifiers to improve performance. This approach involves combining the outputs of these two types of models into a single meta-classifier, trained on error-annotated learner data. By doing so, we aim to address the limitations of the standard approach and develop a more effective error correction system. In the following sections, we will outline our research methodology, describe the specific language models and classifiers we used, and present our experimental results. In addition to comparing the performance of our proposed meta-classification approach to the standard language model and classifier-only scenarios, we will also investigate the effect of training data size on the performance of the meta-classifier. Our study based on a large error-annotated corpus of learner English, which provides a comprehensive picture of errors made by non-native speakers. This corpus contains 1 Million sentence pairs of learner and native English texts, annotated with information about errors as well as their correct counterparts. By analyzing this dataset, we were able to investigate the challenges of error correction in depth and develop our proposed meta-classification approach in response. By combining state-of-the-art language models and errorspecific classifiers with a meta-classifier trained on error-annotated learner data, we were able to achieve substantial gains over the classifier-only and language-model-only scenarios. Furthermore, we found that the meta-classification approach can produce accurate error corrections even with limited training data, making it a more practical solution for applications where large amounts of annotated data are not available. Our results demonstrate the potential of the meta-classification approach for improving error correction performance, and highlight the importance of integrating multiple models and data sources to develop more effective NLP systems. response: Language models are a critical component of many natural language processing (NLP) applications, such as speech recognition, machine translation, and text summarization. They are typically implemented as n-gram models, where the probability of a word being emitted is conditional on a set of previous words. However, as the size of the corpus increases, so does the size of the n-gram model, making it increasingly difficult to store and retrieve the model efficiently (Kneser and Ney, 1995). For example, in a 4-gram language model, the number of possible 3-grams grows exponentially with the size of the vocabulary, leading to significant memory requirements. Consequently, there is an ongoing effort to develop more efficient data structures and algorithms for the implementation of n-gram language models (Schraft and Lennon, 1993;Kuhn and De Mori, 1990). One popular approach for implementing n-gram models is the use of suffix trees (Ukkonen, 1995). A suffix tree is a data structure that can be used to represent a set of strings and is particularly useful for tasks such as string matching and substring extraction. However, constructing and searching suffix trees can be computationally heavy, and storing them in memory can be space-intensive. In this paper, we propose an efficient method for implementing n-gram language models using double-array structures. Our approach has several advantages over traditional suffix tree-based implementations: (1) Reduced memory requirements; (2) Faster query times; and (3) Ease of parallelization. Our method is based on the observation that n-gram models can be represented using a collection of backwards suffix trees. We introduce a double-array structure to represent these suffix trees, where each array stores a suffix link and a next symbol table. The double-array structure is particularly well-suited for storing large n-gram models, as the memory usage grows linearly with the number of suffix nodes and constant with the number of symbols. In addition to the basic double-array structure, we also introduce two optimization techniques to further improve the efficiency of the data representation. The first technique, which we call "probability embedding," reduces the model size by embedding probabilities into free spaces in the array. The second technique, which we call "word ID tuning," optimizes the word IDs in the language model to minimize the reuse of prefixes, thereby reducing the overall size of the model. Traditional automated essay scoring systems employ carefully designed features to evaluate and provide scores for essays. However, the development of a robust automated essay scoring system is challenging and the quality of the system is highly dependent on the availability and quality of features used to evaluate the essays. There are several key challenges associated with designing these systems. The first is the difficulty of defining a comprehensive set of features that effectively capture the complexities of an essay. The second issue is that the development of these features can be time-consuming and requires a significant amount of human judgements to effectively evaluate the essays. Despite these challenges, there have been significant advances made in recent years in developing robust and accurate automated essay scoring systems. One such development has been the use of machine learning techniques, which have the potential to automatically learn the relationship between an essay and its assigned score without requiring any manual feature engineering. response: Event schema induction is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), which aims to automatically identify the underlying structure and relationships in text, specifically in the context of events. Traditional event schema induction methods have focused on extracting event semantics from the head words of a sentence, ignoring the contextual information conveyed by the surrounding words. However, recent work has shown that incorporating contextual information, such as word order and dependencies, can significantly improve event schema induction performance (Chen et al., 2013;Li et al., 2014). In particular, entity disambiguation, which is the task of identifying the correct sense of a word in a given context, plays a crucial role in event schema induction. By accurately identifying the entities involved in an event, we can better understand the relationships and interactions between them, which is essential for capturing event semantics. In this paper, we present a generative model for event schema induction that incorporates entity disambiguation. Our approach builds upon theWeak-sup REM model (WREM) (Li et al., 2014), which has demonstrated strong performance on event schema induction tasks. The WREM model learns a set of latent topics, where each topic represents a specific event schema. However, the WREM model relies on head words to represent entities, which may lead to loss of information and decreased performance. To address this limitation, we propose a novel generative model, called Generative Event Schema Induction with Entity Disambiguation (GESIED), which incorporates entity disambiguation through probabilistic topic distributions. Specifically, we model the entities involved in an event as a set of latent topics, where each topic represents a specific sense of an entity. By learning these entity topics, we can capture the nuanced semantics of entities and improve event schema induction performance. Our proposed model, GESIED, consists of two main components: the entity topic model and the event schema model. However, the rise of user-generated content on the internet has led to a shift towards answering real-world questions from users out of web data. In the real-world setting, the context for a question is not just a single document, but rather full-body text from multiple relevant documents in the top search results. These questions can range from asking for a single, short, and factual answer to seeking reasons, procedures, and opinions. Despite these differences, most existing MRC systems use traditional question-answering mechanisms that are not designed to handle these complexities. In particular, previous systems have focused on addressing the issue of multiple possible answers for a single question by recognizing only one correct answer from a set of possible answers. However, in the real world, multiple answers could be equally valid for a single question. In addition, each answer may occur multiple times in the context, which further complicates the MRC task. The main contribution of this paper is to propose a multi-answer multi-task framework that addresses these challenges. Our framework consists of two key components: a novel multi-answer loss function and a minimum risk training method for handling multi-occurrence answers. In the first component, we use different loss functions for multiple reference answers, which allows us to capture the ambiguities and complexities of real-world questions. The second component, minimum risk training, is used to solve the multi-occurrence problem of a single answer by maximizing the expected reward under different threat models. The goal of JERE is to identify entities andtheir corresponding relations in a given text, which is a fundamental step to derive meaning from unstructured data. Traditional approaches to JERE typically employ a two-stage pipeline: first, extract entities using named entity recognition (NER) models (Ratinov and Roth, 2009); then, use relation extraction models to identify relations between extracted entities (Zhou et al., 2005). One such direction is the use of semantic graphs to represent the meaning of a sentence. Seman- tic graphs can capture the complex interdependencies between entities and relationships in a sentence, and can be tightly coupled with knowledge bases to take advantage of the vast relevant knowledge. On the other hand, another promising direction for semantic parsing is the use of neural network models to map sentences to semantic representations. response: Structured prediction deals with a prediction problem where the input-output pairs are structured objects. This subarea of machine learning has attracted increasing attention in recent years. It usually employs a scoring function $ s_{\theta}(x, y) = f( x | \theta) $, which represents how well the predicted output $ y $ matches the actual output for a given input $ x $, parameterized by the model $ \theta $. A structured prediction task can be formulated as an optimization problem, aiming to find the best output $\hat{y}$ that maximizes $ s_{\theta}(x, y)$ over all possible outputs in the output space. Most existing theory of structured prediction assumes exact inference, where one can accurately compute $ s_{\theta}(x, y)$ and $ \hat{y}(x)$ using this function (Taskar et al., 2004;McAllester, 2003). However, such an assumption is often intractable in many practical problems. For example, even for structured perceptrons, for which we can compute the exact gradient of $ s_{\theta}(x, y)$ with respect to $ \theta$ (Collins, 2002), the exact computation of $ s_{\theta}(x, y)$ and $ \hat{y}(x)$ is still NP-hard for many common structured prediction problems such as structured classification (taskar et al., 2004). As a result, many structured prediction algorithms, including the state-of-the-art systems for part-of-speech tagging and incremental parsing (Vladu et al., 2006;Kim and Manning, 2012), rely on approximate inference heuristics, such as beam search (Chen and Zelle, 1998), which lacks a rigorous theoretical foundation. In this paper, we propose a general framework called the "violation-fixing" perceptrons for structured prediction problems that employ approximate inference heuristics. This framework provides a new separability condition that ensures the convergence of the algorithm under the "early-update" (E-U) rule (Collins and Roark, 2004), one of the most popular heuristics for training perceptrons with beam search. Furthermore, we also propose several new update methods within this framework, which can significantly improve the training speed and the convergence rate of the perceptron. In Section 2, we review some existing work in structured prediction. Previous works on characterizing literary relationships rely heavily on plot summaries that have been manually annotated with predefined labels, such as "friendship" or "romance." However, such an approach has several limitations. Firstly, it is labor-intensive and requires a huge amount of human resources to annotate large datasets. Secondly, even if the annotations are accurate, they might not fully capture the nuances of the relationships. A more flexible and automatic approach is needed to capture the complexities of fictional relationships. Recently, there has been a growing interest in applying machine learning techniques to analyze data from fiction. One of the popular techniques is topic modeling, which is widely used in information retrieval and text analysis (Blei et al., 2003;Hofmann, 1999). Topic models are probabilistic models that decompose a corpus into topics, which are groups of related words in the text. However, topic models are not specifically designed to capture relationships between entities, and hence might not provide accurate results for characterizing dynamic relationships. Another line of research focuses on using graph-based methods to model entities and their relationships (Radev et al., 2009;Kouylekov et al., 2003). These methods can be effective in modeling some types of relationships, but they typically become inadequate when dealing with complex and dynamic relationships. In this work, we propose a novel unsupervised neural network, called RelationTraj, to capture dynamic fictional relationships. RelationTraj jointly learns a set of global relationship descriptors and a trajectory over these descriptors for each relationship in a dataset of raw text from novels. Traditional approaches to semantic parsing, based on symbolic or rule-based representations, are often brittle and require significant manual effort to develop and maintain, making them unsuitable for large-scale requirements elicitation efforts. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in exploring deep learning techniques for semantic parsing tasks, which have shown promising results in modeling the complex relationships between content and context in text. However, most existing works have focused on limited-domain applications, such as question answering or language translation, and have typically employed sentence-level representations that fail to capture the nuanced interactions between individual sentences in context. The ever-growing amount of electronic medical records (EMRs) from different medical specialties urgently demands accurate and efficient medical NER systems. However, the limited availability of labeled data and the variation in terminologies and writing styles across specialties present significant challenges for developing universal medical NER systems (Chen et al., 2013). In particular, the requirement of multi-specialty annotated data is not only expensive, but also impractical due to the vast amount of medical data produced every day, the high cost of human annotation, and the long-latency cycle of data annotation. To alleviate the difficulties, many researchers have proposed using transfer learning to transfer knowledge from an existing NER system with copious amounts of labeled data, to a target system with only limited labeled data. Among these approaches, multi-task learning (Caruana, 1997) and domain adaptation (Blitzer et al., 2007) have received particular attention. However, both of these mainstream methods do not perform well in medical NER due to the relevant label difference between source and target tasks (Shin et al., 2020). Recently, deep multi-task learning models, such as Dunnion et al. (2019), have been designed to tackle this problem. However, they usually still focus on only one thing, parameter transfer, and do not take into account the label differences and transferability between different specialties. In this paper, we tackle the challenge by proposing a novel label-aware double transfer learning framework (La-DTL) tailored for cross-specialty medical NER. (iii) It indicates the possibility of eventually developing universal medical NER systems by leveraging strong learning capabilities in La-DTL. Our future work focuses on applying La-DTL to related applications that involve recurrent temporal and spatial knowledge flow in saga training. This could help uncover common structures that determine progress in medicine. The ultimate goal of grammar induction is to devise an algorithm that can learn a grammar which is both syntactically correct and descriptively adequate from a large corpus of text. Despite the long history, significant progress has been made for inducing dependency grammars in recent years (Goldwater et al., 2006;Goldwater and Johnson, 2003), however the models employed are still overly simplistic, particularly in comparison to supervised parsing models (Klein et al., 2003; Petrov and Klein, 2009). For instance, the approach of Goldwater et al. (2006) defines a random process which samples small phrase structures, which are copied into a grammar through a generative process similar to (Johnson, 2004). While it marks a significant improvement over earlier work on grammar induction and dependency grammar learning, it still lacks the expressiveness found in most successful supervised parsing models, which typically leverage more complex models of local ambiguities in short-range dependencies, such as context-free CFGs, to improve performance. Moreover, the current state-of-the-art models sometimes have high computational costs and heavy memory usage, thus they may not be efficiently applied to parse real-world corpora of some languages. In order to improve on these results, we present an approach to dependency grammar induction which employs tree substitution grammar (Kay, 1980). As with the previous work by (Goldwater et al., 2006), our model starts from the observation that humans rarely need to explicitly represent every possible sentence in a language in order to understand the language: but instead a few common patterns are mixed and combined to generate almost every sentence. However, the previous work by (Goldwater et al., 2006) simply adopts a probabilistic discrete random variable to illustrate the compositional nature of phrase structures, whereas we propose a novel approach that starts with an even lower level of abstraction and depicts the generative process in terms of tree structures. Moreover, the branch of research which studies efficient learning of grandfathered patterns such as positional dependencies of different types is named as word grammars (Ollivierre et al.,2011). In our paper, we also introduce a hierarchical non-parametric Pitman-Yor Process prior to the model, which is initially introduced by (Hewlett et al.,2011), to bias the grammar learnt towards smaller size with simpler productions. There are numerous types of events that can be extracted, including business deals, product launches, accidents, and social movements. Despite the significant advances in event extraction over the past few years, group remaining major challenges persist, particularly when dealing with social media data that lacks context and has an informal tone. The main challenge is extracting meaningful entity and event information from the complex and concise language used in social media. The informal nature of social media data also poses difficulties in accurately determining the entities involved in the event and the relationships between them. Typical event extraction applications using natural language processing (NLP) techniques have shown limited success when dealing with social media data due to the inherent characteristics of this type of data (Chen et al., 2018). Previous work on event extraction for social media often relies on rules-based approaches or machine learning models trained on large amounts of annotated data (Li et al., 2017). However, these approaches fail to capture the contextual information that is crucial for identifying the entities involved in an event, such as speakers, locations, and times. Recent studies have applied knowledge augmentation techniques to improve the performance of event extraction systems (Revow et al., 2000). However, these approaches primarily focus on leveraging external knowledge sources, such as Wikidata or Wikipedia, to enrich the extracted event information with additional facts and metadata. By incorporating knowledge from multiple sources, our approach exploits the contextual information encoded in these sources to boost the accuracy of event extraction. response: Twitter, a microblogging platform with over 330 million active users worldwide (as of April 2023), has become a rich source of information on various events and trends, making it a valuable resource for text mining and topic modeling. The vast amount of user-generated content on Twitter presents both an opportunity and a challenge for topic modeling. On one hand, Twitter data provides a wide range of topics and themes that can be extracted and analyzed using various topic modeling techniques. On the other hand, the short length and ephemeral nature of tweets make it challenging to extract meaningful topics and themes. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed various topic modeling techniques, including the Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) model (Blei et al., 2003). LDA is a popular topic modeling technique that assumes that each document (in this case, a collection of tweets) consists of a mixture of topics, where each topic is a distribution over a set of words (Blei et al., 2003). However, when LDA is applied to Twitter data, it generally treats all aggregated tweets of a user as a single document. This can lead to poor topic modeling results, as it fails to capture the nuances of individual user interests and topic trends. To address this limitation, Twitter-LDA has been proposed (Sasaki et al., 2013). Twitter-LDA assumes that each tweet is a single topic and uses a single topic to represent a tweet. This approach has shown to be superior in topic semantic coherence (Sasaki et al., 2013). However, Twitter-LDA has a major limitation - it is not capable of online inference. Online inference is a critical requirement for topic modeling on Twitter, as it enables the model to adapt to changing user interests and topic trends in real-time. To address this limitation, we propose an online topic model for Twitter that incorporates the dynamics of user interests and topic trends. Our model extends Twitter-LDA in two ways. First, we model the generation process of tweets more accurately by estimating the ratio between topic words and general words for each user. This enables the model to capture the nuances of individual user interests and topic trends. Second, we use the topic tracking model (TTM) (Bradley and Bennett, 2004) to enable online inference. TTM is a probabilistic graphical model that models consumer purchase behaviors, which we adapt to model user interests and topic trends on Twitter. Our proposed model, which we term Online-Twitter-LDA, uses a hierarchical Bayesian framework to capture the dynamics of user interests and topic trends. The model consists of two levels - the user level and the topic level. At the user level, we use a stick-breaking process to model the distribution of topics for each user. At the topic level, we use the Dirichlet process to model the distribution of words for each topic. This enables the model to capture the nuances of individual user interests and topic trends. The contribution of this paper is two-fold. Firstly, we propose an online topic model for Twitter that captures the dynamics of user interests and topic trends. Secondly, we show that our proposed model outperforms existing topic modeling techniques in terms of topic semantic coherence and online inference ability. The experimental results demonstrated that our model is capable of adapt to changing user interests and topic trends in real-time, making it a valuable tool for a wide range of applications, including user profiling, event summarization, and topic tracking.

Reading comprehension, in particular, has been a long-standing challenge in NLP, as it requires a deep understanding of the passage and the ability to directly answer questions based on the information presented in the passage. Despite significant advances in recent years, reading comprehension remains an open problem in NLP. One of the main obstacles to progress is the limited availability of high-quality human-annotated training data. Traditional reading comprehension datasets, such as the MCTest dataset (Richardson et al., 2013), contain only a few hundred training examples, which is insufficient for training large neural networks. To address this issue, Hermann et al. (2015) proposed a novel approach to creating a large-scale reading comprehension dataset. Specifically, they paired news articles from the CNN and Daily Mail with their summarized bullet points to create a large corpus of text passages with question-answer pairs. This corpus, known as the CNN/Daily Mail dataset, contains over a million training examples, making it one of the largest reading comprehension datasets to date. Hermann et al. demonstrated that a neural network can be trained on this dataset to achieve good performance on the reading comprehension task. However, their work left several questions unanswered, including: What depth of language understanding is required to do well on this task? Can simple systems achieve good performance on this task, or do more complex models and sophisticated techniques require? In this paper, we seek to answer these questions and provide a thorough examination of the CNN/Daily Mail reading comprehension task. We approach this problem by taking a two-pronged approach. First, we conduct a careful hand-analysis of a small subset of the problems to understand what language understanding is required to do well on these task. Our analysis reveals that the task requires not only understanding of the passage, but also reasoning and inference abilities. response: Feature representation is a critical component in statistical machine translation (SMT), as it directly influences the performance of the translation model. Generally, features are designed manually based on linguistic knowledge, domain experience, and intuition, and can include a variety of hand-crafted representations, such as phrase translations, tags, and part-of-speech (POS) labels. These features can be manually calculated and are then used to train the SMT model. However, these hand-crafted representations can be time-consuming and costly to develop, and may not effectively capture the complex relationships between different parts of a sentence. Recent advances in deep learning have shown that data-driven representations learned by the model can be more effective and robust than hand-crafted features (Bengio et al., 2003). In particular, the deep autoencoder (DAE) paradigm (Hinton and Salakhutdinov, 2009) has been widely used for unsupervised feature learning. In this paradigm, a deep neural network is trained to reconstruct the input data from a lower-dimensional representation, and in the process, the network learns to capture relevant information about the input data. The learned features can then be used as input to the SMT model. Deep belief nets (DBNs) (Hinton et al., 2006) are a type of feedforward neural network that can be used as a pre-training step for the DAE. DBNs consist of multiple layers of restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs), and the weights of the RBM layers are learned in a hierarchical manner by maximizing the likelihood of the input data. The resulting DBN can be fine-tuned on the labeled data to adjust the weights to match the target supervised task. In this paper, we present a semi-supervised learning approach that learns new features using a DAE paradigm for phrase-based translation models. Our system first pre-trains the deep autoencoder (DAE) parameters using an unsupervised deep belief net (DBN), and then fine-tunes the DAE using the input original phrase features as a teacher for semi-supervised learning. This allows the model to learn the structure of the input data, and the relationships between different parts of a sentence. We also introduce a novel feature composition approach to learn high-dimensional features by combining multiple DAEs. Our approach is data-driven, and the features are learned from the training data without requiring any manual design or engineering effort. Our experiments on two Chinese-English tasks show that our semi-supervised DAE features obtain significant improvements over the unsupervised DBN features and the baseline features, respectively. This demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach in learning more effective and stable features for SMT. There are many benefits to using learning based feature representation for SMT, including requiring less manual design effort, providing the ability to model complex relationships between different parts of a sentence, and helping discover new knowledge about translation tasks. Our results provide evidence that learning based feature representation can be quite effective in improving SMT performance. Another advantage of using learning based features is that they do not require fixed feature definition (Xia, 2006), which are inherently limited to only learnable function types e.g., functions mapping one continuous vector to another continuous vector.assistant In addition, while our current implementation uses the existing phrase-based SMT framework, DAE features have the potential to be directly integrated with other frameworks, such as neural network-based approaches, to further improve translation

Traditional machine learning approaches rely heavily on n-gram models or generic template-based methods, which suffer from low context awareness and limited conversational flexibility. Recent advances in deep learning have led to the development of sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) models, which demonstrate impressive performance in conversational dialogue systems. However, these models do not inherently guarantee the generation of diverse or informative responses, which remains a significant challenge. In this work, we introduce a novel Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) model for neural response generation, which we refer to as GANR. Unlike traditional GAN-based models, our approach incorporates the sequence-to-sequence framework to train a response generative model that modifies existing responses into novel ones. In this framework, the generator is trained to produce a response, and the discriminator is trained to distinguish between human-generated and machine-generated responses. This adversarial process allows the generator to produce highly realistic and diverse responses in short text conversations, without the explicit need to model the target response distribution. Moreover, the GANR framework encourages the generator to produce novel, yet coherent, responses, thus avoiding the problem of safe responses. Furthermore, we introduce an approximate embedding layer to address the sampling-based output decoding procedure in the Seq2Seq generative model. The rising availability of massive amounts of unlabeled text data has enabled the use of text-to-knowledge based entity linking approaches, demonstrating promising performance in entity disambiguation (Wu and Weld, 2010). response: Conversational systems have been widely used in various applications such as customer service, search engines, and chatbots. These systems are generally designed to respond to a specific set of input queries or user requests related to a narrow domain. However, open-domain conversational systems, which are capable of responding to arbitrary and unseen input queries, are less studied although they are highly desirable for real-world applications. When evaluating the performance of conversational systems, metrics such as task accuracy, fluency and naturalness are commonly used. The naturalness of a conversational system is defined as its ability to understand and reflect the nuances and complexities of human communication. However, many of the existing state-of-the-art conversational systems rely heavily on large amounts of pre-defined hand-crafted rules, which are inherently deficient in capturing the complexities of human language. In this paper, we propose a novel open-domain conversational system that is fully based on Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques. Our system, which we call "DeepDialogue", is able to understand and respond to arbitrary input queries without pre-defined rules. This is achieved through a layered architecture, where the input is first analyzed by a natural language analyzer, which identifies the various components of the input, including intent, entities, and context. A dialogue manager is then used to determine the most suitable response based on the analyzed components. We implemented a fully functional DeepDialogue system and conducted a human evaluation study to compare its performance with two other popular conversational systems: a retrieval-based baseline and a rule-based system with 149K hand-crafted rules. Our experimental results showed that DeepDialogue was able to achieve significantly better naturalness than the retrieval-based baseline, while its naturalness is comparable to that of the rule-based system. Furthermore, the human evaluation results revealed that DeepDialogue was preferred by subjects over both baselines in terms of perceived conversational flow and coherence. These results demonstrate that our fully NLP-based architecture is capable of achieving high-quality conversational performance and provide new insights into the design of open-domain conversational systems. response: Event representation learning has been a very active area of research in the natural language processing (NLP) community. A remarkable challenge in this area is learning a robust representation for event patterns that generalize across different domains, entities, and timescales. Most existing methods for learning event representations rely on a large amount of human-annotated event data. While group-level tasks such as event classification can be addressed through weak supervision, tasks that require predicting precise event structures or relationships remain challenging. One of the most significant challenges is that there is a lack of annotated data that not only includes event details but also the relationships among events. Moreover, even data that does include annotations of the relationships between events may lack the intricate relational information needed to model complex event structures. Existing representations for events, such as entity-relation graphs and event jets, fail to capture these complex relationships (Johnson et al., 2008;Ash et al., 2011). Another challenge that makes it hard to learn a robust event representation is the occurrence of rare event patterns. Unlike frequent patterns, which are often in short periodic cycles, rare event patterns exhibit non-periodic patterns, leading to the great difficulty to predict when and where they occur (Kumar, 2004). Considering these challenges, learning a distributed representation for event patterns is essential and has some important applications, such as: (1) preprocessing event discovery: a robust event representation can automatically generate patterns for event discovery: (2) text generation: with such representations, event-based text generation is easier than ever;(3) decision-making systems: by learning a robust event representation, the accuracy and robustness of decision-making systems significantly improve. To learn a robust event representation, we need to tackle the above challenges that almost every proposed solution relies on the human annotation and is restricted to a limited scope of event relationships or is restricted to a limited scope of event patterns. That being the case, few research have been conducted into a model that learns a robust event representation through relatively weak supervision and can extrapolate across both entities and events. To bridge the knowledge gap, we address the above limitations by introducing a novel neural model, called the IDESTmodel. This model utilizes weak supervisions from news published on the same day that mention the same real-world entities. Specifically, given a piece of news that contains one or more event relations, the model tries to learn which entities appeared in that news tweet together with how they related to the news. The relationships can be directional, e.g., Wang proposed a new technology, through or undirectional, e.g., the US stocks fell sharply. We assume that learning both the pairwise distributions of entities and directions of relationships will assist in learning a robust event representation that can extrapollate to rare event patterns and generalize across extractions from different dates. Instead, they may interact with different pages, where various text-span instances may capture different aspects of their interests. Consider a web user who just discovered the impact of climate change on marine ecosystems and is now navigating between online resources to learn more about related topics such as ocean warming and marine life preservation. In this example, a set of text spans, such as the title of a news article or the excerpt of a research paper, incur her interest and lead to subsequent navigation. In data mining and information retrieval research, there is a corresponding interest in predicting user behavior based on page navigation patterns. response: Machine translation (MT) evaluation is a crucial task in the field of natural language processing. MT evaluation metrics are used to estimate the quality of a machine translation system by comparing the produced translation with a human reference translation. Among these metrics, METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005) is particularly popular due to its ability to consider synonymy and morphological similarity between the automatic and reference translations. However, METEOR has limitations in understanding the potential subtleties in language. To overcome these limitations and provide a more comprehensive evaluation, researchers have proposed integrating external lexico-semantic resources into MT evaluation metrics. One such approach is the use of lexical resources like WordNet (Fellbaum, 1998) and DBnary (Navigli, 2009). By incorporating these resources, evaluation metrics can identify meanings that may not be explicitly mentioned but can be inferred through the use of lexical and semantic relationships. Nevertheless, these resources require significant storage and updating efforts to stay current. Recent advances in word representation techniques have provided an alternative for augmenting MT evaluation metrics. Pre-trained vector representations, such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), have been shown to capture certain nuances in language. These vectors have been found to be effective in capturing similar semantic relationships as lexical resources. However, the real challenge is deciding which type of augmenting method to use: incorporating lexico-semantic resources or distributed representations of words. In this paper, we investigate the impact of both approaches on the performance of METEOR in evaluating machine translations. Our experiments are conducted in the context of the Metrics task of the Workshop on Machine Translation (WMT) 2014. We consider the metrics tasks of translating news stories from German and Czech into English. We compare the results of the augmented METEOR versions using vector representations and DBnary. The results of our experiments show that the distributed representations are a good alternative to lexical resources, bringing interesting additional information to the METEOR evaluation metric. Specifically, the effectiveness of vector representations in revealing more subtle semantic relationships becomes more apparent in longer sentences, pointing out the usefulness of static lexical representations as an alternative. Emotion recognition in text is crucial for natural language processing applications such as sentiment analysis, affective computing, and opinion mining. While sentiment is a global evaluation of a text (negative or positive), emotions are more nuanced groupings within that global sentiment and can involve subtle and context-dependent feelings or intuitions (Moore and Piringer, 2007). Emotion classification from text relies heavily on word-emotion association, but existing emotion lexicons incur several disadvantages. Firstly, they are generally limited in their coverage of emotions and the words they pair with these emotional categories (Mohammad, 2018). This paucity of depth and breadth may therefore lead to shallow insights and a narrow perspective on emotions. Recently, the encoder-decoder framework has achieved significant success in image captioning, where the encoder extracts a set of relevant features from the input image, and the decoder generates a sequence of words to form the caption. To overcome the challenges of generating detailed and comprehensive captions, researchers have explored various techniques to fuse visual information and linguistic context. Visual attention mechanisms have been widely adopted to focus on salient regions of the image, while semantic attention processes topical information to provide a broader and more abstract understanding of the scene. In this paper, we propose the Stepwise Image-Topic Merging Network (simNet) to address these limitations. Unlike previous methods that mainly focus on a single modality or separate the visual and semantic information, we propose to integrate these two pieces of information in a stepwise and adaptive manner. response: Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) is a central task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in a wide range of downstream tasks, such as question answering, sentiment analysis, and text classification. Given two texts, STS aims to score their semantic similarity on a scale of 0 (completely dissimilar) to 5 (equivalent in meaning). However, despite the existence of hundreds of STS systems, selecting the best one for a particular task remains a challenging problem for NLP system designers. This is largely due to the fact that current evaluation methods often rely on intrinsic evaluation, which compares the output of the STS system to human judgments on semantic similarity. While intrinsic evaluation using metrics such as Pearson correlation has been widely adopted, we argue that it may not be the most effective choice for evaluating STS systems. In this paper, we investigate the pitfalls of relying on Pearson correlation for intrinsic evaluation and propose a framework for conducting a more nuanced and task-oriented evaluation. We contend that a task-oriented approach is essential to selecting the most suitable STS system for a particular NLP task. By examining the properties of the targeted task, we can design an evaluation framework that takes into account the specific requirements of the task and thus yields more accurate results. Our approach is to decompose the task into subtasks, each with its unique characteristics, and then evaluate STS systems based on their performance on these subtasks. This multi-faceted evaluation approach allows us to gain a deeper understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each system and make a more informed decision about which one to use. We illustrate the benefits of our approach using three common STS-based tasks: question answering, sentiment analysis, and text classification. Our results demonstrate that Pearson correlation, while useful in some cases, is not always the most appropriate metric for evaluating STS systems. Furthermore, we show that other metrics, such as Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (ρ), often provide a more accurate assessment of system performance. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. In Section 2, we discuss the challenges of STS evaluation and the limitations of current methods. In Section 3, we propose a framework for conducting task-oriented intrinsic evaluation of STS systems. In Section 4, we present our experimental setup and results, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. These tasks have led to significant advancements in the field of computer vision and natural language processing, with a focus on developing attentive and end-to-end trainable models. Despite these advancements, there has been much less work on video-based QA, partly due to the availability of high-quality, large-scale datasets that span long periods of video content. The majority of existing video-based QA datasets (e.g., TACoS (Rohrbach et al., 2014), MSVD (Xu et al., 2017), and TVSummary (Zhang et al., 2017)) have significant limitations, such as small dataset size, short video clips, and simple questions that focus on object detection, scene recognition, and basic language understanding. To address this gap, we have created TVQA, a large-scale video QA dataset based on six popular TV shows. TVQA consists of 152,545 QA pairs from 21,793 clips, spanning over 460 hours of video. Questions in the dataset are designed to be compositional in nature, requiring systems to jointly localize relevant moments within a clip, comprehend subtitle-based dialogue, and recognize relevant visual concepts. response: Machine translation (MT) systems have been widely used in various applications such as translation of web pages, documentation, and communication among people with different languages. However, the assessment of MT quality has been a challenging task. Traditional methods of evaluating MT quality often rely on a single metric, such as Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) (Papineni et al., 2002), which focuses on the precision and recall of translating n-grams. These approachesconsider only a particular aspect of translation quality and may not be effective in evaluating other valuable aspects such as fluency, coherence, and style. As MT systems improve, the need for more sophisticated evaluation metrics becomes more pressing. Researchers have proposed new metrics, such as Smoothed Non- Isomorphic Ratio (SNIR), which evaluates the fluency of a translation by comparing it to a predefined fluency reference (Chen et al., 2009), and Automatic Postediting (APE), which evaluates the quality of a translation by checking whether automatic postediting can improve it (Popovic and Ney, 2013). However, manually tuning these metrics to obtain the optimal trade-off between the different metric values is often highly time-consuming and imperfect. This has led to another problem: metric tunability. With multiple evaluation metrics, how do we choose the optimal combination of metrics? It is clear that ad hoc methods such as simply assigning weights to each metric are highly subjective and may not always result in good translations. The necessity for a more principled approach led to our investigation of multi-objective optimization for machine translation. In this paper, we show that by using the Pareto optimality theory, we can learn a translation model that is better than the individual models optimized for single metrics. Pareto optimality is a concept from economics that has been widely used in multi-objective optimization. It is defined as the set of solutions that simultaneously minimize the maximum value over all objectives. In other words, Pareto optimal solutions are relatively better than others with respect to at least one objective. The main advantage of using Pareto optimality for multi-objective optimization is that it can produce a set of trade-off solutions, each of which optimizes a different aspect of translation quality. In our implementation, we use the machine learning algorithms of maximum expected recall (MERT) (Och and Ney, 2003) and adaptive multi-metric optimization (AMO) (Hildebrandt et al., 2014) as the base optimization methods. By applying the Pareto optimality theory to these methods, we obtain the Pareto-frontier, which consists of the distributions of translation quality metrics on both test sets. Our approach has several advantages over ad hoc linear combination of metrics: Firstly, it is much easier to implement on top of existing single-objective optimization methods; Secondly, our approach is more effective in incorporating new metrics from MT evaluation, since we can adjust the set of metrics dynamically in the Pareto optimality algorithm.assistant Our evaluation results demonstrate the effectiveness of our Pareto-based multi-objective optimization for machine translation. We use a standard dataset for machine translation evaluation, IWSLT 2014, with a test set consisting of 4000 sentences and four evaluation metrics: BLEU-4, Meteor, TER, and HDet (D Series), representing fluency, coherence, and style. We compare our approach with the state-of-the-art single-objective models optimized for individual metrics

The goal of WSD is to assign the most appropriate sense to an ambiguous word in a given context, and the success of any WSD approach largely depends on the use of accurate and discriminative features. Traditional supervised WSD approaches rely on features that capture the semantic meaning of a word, such as its synonyms, hyponyms, and hypernyms, as well as its syntactic properties, such as its part-of-speech tag and grammatical function. However, these traditional features often suffer from several limitations. Firstly, they require a large amount of annotated training data, which can be extremely expensive and time-consuming to acquire, especially for fine-grained sense distinctions. Secondly, they can be overconfident, relying too heavily on the selected set of features and neglecting other relevant information in the context. Finally, they can be inflexible, failing to adapt to changes in the context or the domain. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach to supervised WSD that incorporates a new class of features, which we refer to as selectors. Compounds, which are words formed from two or more morphemes, are a common phenomenon in many languages, including German. In German, compounds can be either agglutinative, combining two independent words, or inflectional, forming a new word by combining an adjective with a noun. German compounds can be split into subgroups based on the position of the unstressed syllable, which is a key characteristic of this type of compoundization in German. Compounds can exhibit a range of relationships, such as hierarchical, sequential, and thematic, each of which may influence the meaning of the resulting compound. Compositionality is the idea that the meaning of a complex expression is a function of the meaning of its components and the way they are combined. In the context of language modeling and artificial intelligence, compositionality is a key property that allows for the creation of more sophisticated models that can generalize to new, unseen data. Composition models aim to predict the meaning of complex expressions from the meaning of their components in various types of expression, such as phrases, sentences, or words. In the case of German compounds, composition models can be used to predict the meaning of a compound from the meanings of its immediate constituents. Reversing the process and trying to "reverse-engineer" the language can provide valuable insights into how language is structured and how compositionality operates. If we can use a vector space model, like the word embeddings, to first represent the German language and to estimate the corpusestimated vector for a compound, then we can try to use various composition models to compose the representations of the immediate constituents to obtain a predicted representation for the compound. We can then compare the observed representation with the predicted representation and assess the performance of the different composition models in terms of how well they recreate the observed representation. By simultaneously predicting syntax and semantics, SAMT aims to capture the complex interplay between the two, yielding more accurate and coherent translations. A key component of SAMT is the use of a rich and expressive label set to represent the syntactic structure of sentences. This label set, often consisting of hundreds of categories, is typically learned through unsupervised or weakly-supervised methods (Li et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2019). However, as the size of the label set increases, so does the risk of sparsity and ambiguity problems. These issues arise when categories are underrepresented or confused with one another, leading to poor translation quality and increased computational complexity. To mitigate these problems, we propose a novel approach to inducing label coarsening in SAMT grammars. Our method, Category Coarsening for Syntax-Augmented Machine Translation (CC-SAMT), leverages a tree-to-tree grammar coarsening algorithm (Brebner and Ng, 2017) to reduce the label set size while preserving the original grammar's expressive power. Predicate-argument structure is the underlying semantic representation of a sentence, which can be used in a wide range of NLP applications, such as question answering (Zhang et al., 2006), text summarization (Nunez-Miret et al., 2012), and sentiment analysis (Wong et al., 2010). SRL is an active area of research in NLP, with various approaches proposed in recent years (Kordjamshid et al., 2015;Schmitt and Lapata, 2018;Zhong et al., 2019). While the advent of deep learning has seen significant improvements in SRL performance (Bartoletti et al., 2016;Chen et al., 2018;Lu et al., 2019), the role of syntactic information, which is often identified as a key determinant of argument structure, remains unclear. In fact, a recent line of work has demonstrated that neural SRL models can achieve impressive performance without explicitly modeling syntactic information, raising questions about the necessity of syntactic information in SRL (Ma and Hovy, 2016;Xu et al., 2019). These studies suggest that neural models may be able to implicitly learn the relevant syntactic information from the data, obviating the need for explicit modeling. However, this perspective has been challenged by a growing body of evidence indicating that syntactic information can have a significant impact on SRL performance (Ji et al., 2017;Schmitt and Lapata, 2018). In this work, we aim to quantify the importance of syntactic information in dependency SRL, a major subtask of SRL, which focuses on identifying the arguments of the predicate, typically represented as a dependency graph (Meyers et al., 2004). response: The representation of word meaning has been a long-standing problem in the field of linguistics and artificial intelligence. Traditional approaches to word meaning have relied heavily on linguistic information, such as co-occurrence patterns and lexical definitions. However, there is growing evidence that language is not grounded solely in the linguistic environment, but rather is deeply rooted in perception and action (Lakoff, 1987;Jackendoff, 1987). This has led to the development of a range of grounded models of semantic representation that attempt to capture the relationships between language, perception, and action. In spite of this shift in perspective, the use of linguistic data remains ubiquitous in the field. Language models, for example, rely heavily on large corpora of text to learn the meanings of individual words and phrases (Collobert et al., 2011;Mikolov et al., 2013). However, this focus on linguistic data can often lead to a narrow and superficial representation of word meaning, one that neglects the rich percepts and actions that underlie human experience. In recent years, there has been growing interest in the use of perceptual data, such as feature norms, to inform semantic representation (Ciborra, 1996;Kiefski, 2013). Feature norms describe the attributes that native speakers consider important in describing the meaning of a word, such as color, texture, or shape. This type of data can capture the nuanced and multidimensional nature of word meaning, and has been shown to be effective in a range of semantic tasks (Lenci, 2008). However, even when using perceptual data, the integration of linguistic and perceptual information remains a significant challenge. In general, linguistic and perceptual data are encoded in very different modalities, and it is unclear how to effectively combine them in a single model (De Leeuw et al., 2008). This can result in a fragmented or disjointed representation of word meaning, one that fails to capture the full richness and complexity of human experience. Traditional approaches to these tasks have attempted to model them as separate and distinct subproblems, each with its own optimization criteria, loss functions, and evaluation metrics. Traditional methods of information retrieval rely on simple statistical models, such as bag-of-words (BOW), that treat each document as a single vector of word frequency and do not capture the inherent structure of the text data. This approach has been widely used for a long time, but it suffers from the limitations of being unable to model relationships between words, and it fails to capture the topical structure of the text. The rising popularity of virtual assistants like Siri, Alexa, and Google Assistant has fueled the need for more sophisticated and realistic conversation models. As users interact with these systems, they often expect meaningful and informative responses that acknowledge the context of the conversation and address the user"s specific questions or requests. One popular approach to building generative conversation systems is through the use of Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) models, which leverage neural networks to generate responses based on the input question or prompt. However, even with the power of Seq2Seq models, generative conversation systems often fall short of delivering truly meaningful and informative responses, typically resorting to generic or trivial answers that fail to engage the user. One major challenge in addressing this limitation is the restrictive nature of the standard Seq2Seq architecture, which focuses primarily on learning the co-occurrence of words in a sequence without considering more nuanced aspects of language, such as context, implication, and inferences. In an effort to break away from this limitation, we propose an innovative approach to implicit content-introducing for generative short-text conversation systems. Our approach focuses on incorporating additional information into the Seq2Seq model in a flexible and context-aware manner. The core idea is to blend general decoding with auxiliary cue word information, drawing inspiration from the human thought process when generating responses. In essence, we propose the use of a hierarchical gated fusion unit to amalgamate these two components and generate more informed and context-specific replies. By leveraging the strengths of both components, our model can adapt to a wide range of conversation contexts and themes, leading to more satisfying and informative conversations. We conduct a series of experiments on real-life data to demonstrate the effectiveness of our model, both in terms of quantitative metrics like BLEU scores and human evaluation metrics. The results indicate that our implicit content-introducing approach leads to consistent improvements across various baselines, underscoring the potential for our approach to inform future developments in the field of generative conversation systems. The success of our model can be attributed to the unique aspects of our hierarchical gated fusion unit, which allows for a seamless integration of general decoding and auxiliary cue word information. Aspect-level sentiment classification (ALSC), a specific form of sentiment analysis, focuses on predicting the sentiment polarity of a certain product aspect mentioned in a text, such as "value" or "price." ALSC is a more challenging task than traditional sentiment analysis since it not only requires determining the overall sentiment but also identifying the specific aspect under consideration. Although they differ in their focus and scale, both techniques aim to capture meaningful patterns and relationships within data. General-purpose topic models, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), aim to group similar documents or sentences into topics based on their word co-occurrence patterns (Blei et al., 2003). However, these models work at a relatively coarse granularity, neglecting the subtle nuances and context-dependent relationships between words. Word embedding models, on the other hand, focus on modeling word co-occurrence within small sliding windows, capturing fine-grained semantic relationships between words (Mikolov et al., 2013). Word embeddings have proven to be highly effective in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, such as word similarity, sentiment analysis, and machine translation. However, they are primarily designed for word-level modeling and lack the ability to capture larger-scale semantic relationships between topics. In this paper, we propose a novel model called Latent Topic Embedding (LTE), which integrates topic generation and word embedding learning in a unified framework. By leveraging the strengths of both topic modeling and word embedding, LTE captures word co-occurrence information at different levels of granularity, ultimately deriving more informative and representational latent topics. The integration of topic modeling and word embedding in LTE has several benefits. Firstly, it enables the capture of topic-level semantics, allowing for more accurate topic modeling. CWS is usually done by training a conditional random field (CRF) over a labeled dataset, where each token in the sentence is assigned to a specific position and features are extracted around each token to group them together as a whole word. This task is challenging because the rules for Chinese word segmentation are complex and do not apply uniformly across different domains (Li et al., 2010). Besides, new words emerge constantly in Chinese, which poses a challenge to CWS systems. New word detection is a subtask of CWS that aims at discovering new words in addition to existing ones. Existing methods for CWS generally rely on labeled training data and can fall short of performance when dealing with out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words, especially when the system encounters a new word for the first time. This lack of OOV ability is a shortcoming of many existing approaches to CWS and new word detection. In existing methods, word-based features are often used as the primary means to represent features around each token. Word-based features contain linguistic information relevant for word segmentation, such as word shape, word bigram or trigram, word type, and chunk tag. Examples of word-based features comprise: word as a binary vector, word as a multi-hot vector (GDI), word as a multi-dimensional vector, and word list matching scheme (Li et al., 2009). Word-based features are although successful in capturing linguistic features relevant for word segmentation, but fall short in terms of robustness and applicability. For example, it is hard to extract word roots from Chinese words that contain simplifications of complex characters and punctuation marks. Traditional word representation learning models, like Word2Vec and GloVe, directly take the entire corpus as training data and group words together based on their co-occurrence patterns. However, ignoring the varying complexity of instances in the corpus may lead to sub-optimal representations, especially when the corpus consists of a large number of instances. The complexity of instances can be due to various factors, including the presence of multiple co-references, the abundance of temporal or spatial information, or the varying lengths of sentences.
